newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Crompton fights off foreign competition.
newsitem.headline: India's Crompton fights off foreign competition.

text.p: The prospect of competition, especially from foreign companies, scares many Indian firms, but Crompton Greaves Ltd has proved that it can take on the international big boys and win.

India's largest private sector electrical equipment maker has held its own against global majors such as Asea Brown Boveri Ltd (ABB), Siemens India Ltd and GEC Alsthom India Ltd on the back of its core engineering strength and distribution network, analysts said.
Industrial and power systems account for more than 70 percent of its total sales.

"In its power systems and industrial systems group, Crompton Greaves has competed with heavyweights like ABB, BHEL (Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd) and Siemens for many years and yet it remains a dominant player," said analyst Sunil Mohindra at Kotak Securities.
Analysts say the firm is a good play in the Indian power generation and distribution sector where industrial growth is likely to spur huge demand.
"Crompton Greaves is expected to be a major beneficiary of buoyant industrial growth," brokerage firm, James Capel B&K said in a report on India's top 100 companies.
The firm manufactures transformers, motors, switch gears, telecommunications equipment and consumer products.
Crompton has 28 manufacturing plants spread over 11 centres in India and employs 12,000 workers.
The company has restructured its operations into four Strategic Business Units (SBUs) in a bid to boost turnover and enhance competitiveness.
It reported a net profit of 558.2 million rupees ($15.66 million) and sales of 15 billion in the year to March 31, 1996.
"Crompton Greaves's recent restructuring into four SBUs is likely to enhance its competitiveness and help reduce overheads, thereby expanding margins," Kotak's Mohindra said in a report.
Power systems, customer products, industrial systems and digital activities will be Crompton's four main focus groups.

The Thapar group, which runs the firm, has interests in paper, glass, chemicals and man-made fibres. It owns about 32 percent of Crompton's equity while Britain's BTR Plc holds 16 percent. Foreign institutional investors hold another 24 percent of the stock.

The company has a history of collaboration with world leaders in its related businesses. It is currently conducting a feasibility study with Germany's Bausch AG with a view to manufacturing washing machines.

"(Crompton's) main competitive advantage lies in its core engineering strengths derived from low-cost technical manpower. Tie-ups with global majors .... have facilitated the assimilation of the latest technologies," Kotak said.
"We hope to record a turnover of 20 billion rupees by 1997-98 and are aiming for 40 billion rupees by the year 2,000," Crompton's vice-president for communications A. Dasgupta said.

"Massive investments in human resource development and extensive marketing networks has made us a major player," he told Reuters. "We expect growth to continue in our conventional areas along with additions in our diversified focus areas."
Crompton's $50 million Euroissue in June priced at a premium drew commitments for nearly nine times the offer reflecting strong foreign investor demand.

"We expect Crompton Greaves to benefit from its strong leadership positions in key products catering to three major sectors of the growing Indian economy -- power, heavy industry and consumer durables," securities firm H.G. Asia said.
